challenge.name: NAND circuit checker on a custom CPU (Pachinko / Pachinko Revisited)

all_of: user-supplied indices are bounds-checked and then arithmetically transformed before being used as an address
the transformed address is applied to a memory space that also holds code
any_of: the check is against the pre-scaling value rather than the final address
the address space wraps at a machine word so a large value folds back to a low region
the interpreter and its program share one flat address space

chain.action: read the client bundle for the submission format and the real goal, and treat unreferenced constants as dead code
chain.why: the client referenced GOALS.xor while only GOALS.flip existed; believing the former wastes the whole first flag

chain.action: map the accepted id range from the server's own rejections rather than from the UI
chain.why: the boundary (1..65535 at the transport, <0x1000 at the checker) is where the two validators disagree

chain.action: stop probing variants once one mechanism class produces no distinguishing signal, and change layer
chain.why: unassigned nodes all read 0; ~50% of ids pass a single oracle trial by chance, which manufactures false leads

chain.action: pick an index whose post-scaling address wraps into instruction memory and use it as a 2-byte arbitrary write
append the privileged routine's own instructions after the processing loop so the CPU executes them before halting
chain.why: the program never calls flag_magic itself; the write supplies the call

first_confirming_probe.request: submit the minimal correct circuit, then the same circuit with one node id just past the checker's documented limit, and compare the two responses
first_confirming_probe.expected: the correct circuit returns the success output while the out-of-range id is rejected by a different layer, proving two validators with different limits
first_confirming_probe.falsifier: both are rejected identically, meaning a single validator governs the id and no scaling gap exists

blast_radius: read-only against a per-user instance; the checker is invoked per request and a few hundred gates is enough, so there is no need to send large circuits.

verification.evidence: both flags were returned in the flag field of the live POST /check JSON response

reuse_when: a bounds check is applied before an index is scaled, shifted or multiplied
an interpreter stores code and data in one address space that wraps at a machine word
a challenge ships an emulator rather than a native binary
known_traps: the client references a goal that does not exist; read which one the server actually checks
the checker evaluates ONE random input vector per request, so a circuit that is only sometimes correct passes intermittently -- always repeat a trial before believing it
an oracle with a 50% pass rate manufactures false positives in proportion to how many ids you scan; six confirmation trials still leaves ~1 false positive per 64 candidates
